```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
#loading data
df = read.csv("data/SeoulBikeData.csv", fileEncoding = "latin1") %>% clean_names() %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date, format = "%d/%m/%Y"))

#making temperature groups
df_temp_mean <- df %>% 
  mutate(temp_grp = factor(
    case_when(
      temperature_c <= -10 ~ "< -10",
      temperature_c >= -10 & temperature_c < 0 ~ "-10 - 0",
      temperature_c >= 0 & temperature_c < 10 ~ "0 - 10",
      temperature_c >= 10 & temperature_c < 20 ~ "10 - 20",
      temperature_c >= 20 & temperature_c < 30 ~ "20 - 30",
      temperature_c >= 30 & temperature_c < 40 ~ "30 - 40",
      TRUE ~ "> 40" 
      ), 
    level = c("< -10",
              "-10 - 0",
              "0 - 10", 
              "10 - 20", 
              "20 - 30", 
              "30 - 40", 
              "> 40"))) %>% 
  group_by(temp_grp) %>% 
  summarise(mean_bike_count = mean(rented_bike_count, na.rm= TRUE))

#trialdf6 -> df_bike_temp
df_bike_temp <- df %>% 
  select(date, rented_bike_count, temperature_c, seasons) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(day_bike_count = sum(rented_bike_count), 
            mean_day_temp_c = mean(temperature_c))

#trialdf7 -> df_bike_humid
df_bike_humid <- df %>% 
  select(date, humidity, seasons, rented_bike_count) %>% mutate(
  date = as.Date(date)
)%>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(day_bike_count = sum(rented_bike_count), 
            mean_day_humidity = mean(humidity))

#trialdf8 -> df_bike_rain
df_bike_rain <- df %>% 
  select(date, rainfall_mm, seasons, rented_bike_count) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(day_bike_count = sum(rented_bike_count), 
            mean_day_rainfall = mean(rainfall_mm))

#trialdf12 -> df_bike_season
df_bike_season = df %>% select(-functioning_day, -holiday) %>% mutate(seasons = factor(seasons, levels = c("Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Autumn"))) %>% group_by(date, seasons) %>% 
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(rented_bike_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#trialdf13 -> df_temp_season
df_temp_season = df %>% select(-functioning_day, -holiday) %>% mutate(seasons = factor(seasons, levels = c("Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Autumn"))) %>% group_by(date, seasons) %>% 
  summarise(
    m = mean(temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#trialdf14 -> humid_temp
humid_temp = inner_join(df_bike_humid, df_bike_temp, by = c("day_bike_count", "date"))

#trialdf15 -> df_sunlight
df_sunlight <- df%>% 
  select(date, rented_bike_count, solar_radiation_mj_m2)%>% 
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(
    hours_of_sunlight=sum(solar_radiation_mj_m2 > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_bike_count= mean(rented_bike_count))

#bike_sun_df
bike_sun_df <- df_sunlight %>%
  group_by(date, hours_of_sunlight) %>%
  summarise(day_bike_count = sum(rented_bike_count))

#trialdf18 -> tempdf
tempdf <- left_join(humid_temp, df_bike_rain, by = c("date", "day_bike_count"))
  daily_weather_bike <- left_join(tempdf, bike_sun_df, by  = c("date", "day_bike_count"))

```


## Research Question

Our research question, ‘To what extent can variation in bike demand throughout the year in Seoul be attributed to changes in weather?’ aims to explore and model how different weather related factors affect fluctuations in bike demand in Seoul from the given data frame. This question might be of interest to local governing bodies when designing infrastructure or bike sharing companies that might want to optimise pricing and distribution of bikes.


## Data

Our investigation uses the Seoul Bike Sharing Demand dataset by UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository with 14 variables and 8760 observations, consisting of readings over every hour of every day between the dates 01/12/2017 and 30/11/2018. 

We used the following variables in the initial dataset in our exploration:

```{r variables table, echo = FALSE}
key_vars <- tibble(Variable = c("date", "rented_bike_count", "hour", "temperature_c", "humidity", "rainfall_mm", "seasons", "solar_radiation"), Type = c("date", "integer", "integer", "continuous", "integer", "integer", "categorical", "continuous"), Description = c("date when recordings with taken", "hourly number of rented bikes", "hour of the day", "recorded temperature in degrees celsius", "recorded humidity as a percentage", "recorded rainfall in millimetres", "winter, spring, summer or autumn", "recorded solar radiation in megajoules per metre squared"))

kable(key_vars)

```

```{r table1, echo = FALSE}

       Type = c( "numeric (double)", "factor with 7 levels", "numeric (integer)", "numeric (double)", " numeric (double)", "numeric (double)", "numeric (integer)"),
```

### Assumptions and Limitations:
When importing the dataset from excel into the R Studio project, the Date variable data type was converted into string rather than retaining its original format, so we performed data cleaning and transformation (in the form of as.Date()) to ensure all variables were suitable for analysis and effective plotting of data.

Since we decided to measure the influence of predictors on a bike demand (a numerical variable), we were limited to using linear regression when it came to modelling as logistic regression is only suitable for predicting categorical variables. 

During the exploration of the data it seemed there might be some anomalous values in our outcome variable, such as several days with a 0 rented bike count at all hours or some extremely high counts at some hours. However, after reviewing a boxplot below of all hourly rented bike counts, we decided to keep these values in our analysis as it would not make sense to remove the high bike counts.

```{r boxplot, echo = FALSE}
ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = rented_bike_count))+
  geom_boxplot()

```

### Exploration & Visualisations:
#### 1. Temperature and Bike Demand

```{r temp v bikes, echo = FALSE}
coeff <- 0.001

ggplot(data = df_bike_temp, mapping = aes(x = date)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = day_bike_count), 
             colour = "tomato", size = 1, alpha = 0.4) + 
  geom_smooth(aes(y = day_bike_count), se = FALSE, 
              colour = "tomato", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mean_day_temp_c/ coeff), 
             colour = "cornflowerblue", size = 1, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = mean_day_temp_c/ coeff), se = FALSE, 
              colour = "cornflowerblue", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Date",
       title = "Correlation Between Number of Rented Bikes and Temperature") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Number of Rented Bikes",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~.*coeff, name="Temperature (in degrees celsius)")
  )+
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_text(color = "tomato", size = 13),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "cornflowerblue", size = 13)
  ) 

#by season


coeff = 0.025

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df_bike_season, aes(x = date, y = Mean), stat = "identity", colour = "orchid", size = 2, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(data = df_bike_season, aes(x = date, y = Mean), se = FALSE, colour = "orchid") +
  geom_point(data = df_temp_season, aes(x = date, y = m/coeff),colour = "palevioletred", size = 2, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(data = df_temp_season, aes(x = date, y = m/coeff), se = FALSE,colour = "palevioletred") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Mean Rented Bike Count",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~.*coeff, name="Mean Temperature (C)")
  )+
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_text(colour = "orchid", size=13),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(colour = "palevioletred", size=13)
  ) +
  
  labs(
    x = "Date",
    title = "Effect Temperature has on Rented Bike Count per Day"
  ) + 
  facet_wrap(~ seasons, scales = "free_x") 

```

Both graphs illustrate the relationship between number of rented bikes and temperature throughout the year, except that Figure 1 examines the overall trend across the whole year whereas Figure 2 separates the data into four seasons, allowing seasonal variations to be explored and viewed in greater detail. Both graphs show that generally as temperature increases, so does bike demand implying that there is a relationship between warmer weather and greater demand for rental bikes. 

Although the graphs suggest an association, this does not prove that temperature directly influences bike rental demand as correlation does not imply causation. Additionally, both graphs follow a similar trend, peaking in the summer (in the middle of the year) with either end of the year dipping to lower bike rental counts and lower temperatures. Both graphs also show a peak of both bike rentals and temperature during the summer period, but this is particularly visible in the initial graph; yet from this graph there is a distinct difference in the peaks between bike rentals and temperature, suggesting that temperature does not fully explain the variation in bike rental demand. The second graph breaks down the data in 4 segments to get a more precise reading and trend per season, showing a clear and distinct positive relationship in spring and more.
The Pearson correlation coefficient for Figure 1 was calculated to be 0.69982 to 5 significant figures, suggesting a moderately strong linear relationship between the two variables, supporting the relationship deduced from the first graph; however the value is not strong enough for temperature to be the only variable affecting bike rental demand. 

This can be further attested to by the graph below which measures the mean bike count for each temperature group:

```{r temp bar, echo = FALSE}

ggplot(data = df_temp_mean, aes(x = temp_grp, y = mean_bike_count, fill = "salmon" ))+
  geom_col()+
  theme_bw()+
  labs(x = "Temperature group (degrees celsius)",
       y = "Number of Rented Bikes", 
       title = "Rented bike count by temperature group")+
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
#### 2. Humidity and Bike Demand

```{r humidity v bikes, echo = FALSE}
#Correlation between Humidity and Bike Demand

coeff <- 0.001

ggplot(df_bike_humid, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = day_bike_count), colour = "hotpink", size = 0.6) + 
  geom_smooth(aes(y = day_bike_count), se = FALSE, colour = "hotpink", size = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mean_day_humidity/ coeff), colour = "chartreuse4", size = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = mean_day_humidity/ coeff), se = FALSE, colour = "chartreuse4", size = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Date",
       title = "Correlation Between Number of Rented Bikes and Mean Humidity") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Number of Rented Bikes",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~.*coeff, name="Humidity (%)")
  )+
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_text(color = "hotpink", size=13),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "chartreuse4", size=13)
  ) 

df_bike_humid %>% summarise(Correlation = cor(day_bike_count, mean_day_humidity))
```
Here, we observed the relationship between the number of bikes rented daily and the mean humidity of that day. In the above figure, both graphs peak and fall at around the same time, following similar trends implying that as mean humidity increases the number of bikes demanded in a day increases as well. However, while the data points for the number of rented bikes remain, for the most part, close to their associated graph, we can see that the data points for humidity rarely follow the plotted line. This tells us that humidity does not follow a recognisable trend over the year leading its graph to be underfitted. Additionally, the pearson correlation coefficient of 0.028 tells us that there is a positive but very weak correlation between humidity and number of bikes demanded in a day.

#### 3. Rainfall and Bike Demand

```{r bike v rainfall, echo = FALSE}
coeff <- 0.0001

ggplot(df_bike_rain, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = day_bike_count), colour = "violetred", size = 0.6) + 
  geom_smooth(aes(y = day_bike_count), se = FALSE, colour = "violetred", size = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mean_day_rainfall/ coeff), colour = "royalblue4", size = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = mean_day_rainfall/ coeff), se = FALSE, colour = "royalblue4", size = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Date",
       title = "Correlation Between Number of Rented Bikes and Mean Rainfall for a Day") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Number of Rented Bikes",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~.*coeff, name="Rainfall (mm)")
  )+
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_text(color = "violetred", size=13),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "royalblue4", size=13)
  ) 

df_bike_rain %>% summarise(Correlation = cor(day_bike_count, mean_day_rainfall))

```

Above, we plotted the graphs for the number of rented bikes in a day and the mean rainfall for that day measured in millimetres. From the graphs it appears that there is no visible relationship between the demand for bikes and rainfall, as the demand rises and falls as rainfall remains almost constant at low levels with few exceptions. This is seen in a low Pearson correlation coefficient of -0.214 which tells us there is a negative and weak relationship between rainfall and bikes demanded. The boxplot below shows that most, if not, all of the non-zero values in the rainfall variable are anomalous, making it almost impossible to make a reliable model to predict bike count from rainfall. Hence, we decided not to include rainfall as a predictor in our models.

```{r rain boxplot, echo = FALSE}
```
